claims.text: Quality is the degree to which a product meets the customer's expectations, judged by fitness for purpose against the price paid, rather than by expensive materials alone.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Quality production matters to a business because poor output tends to drive customers to rivals and to raise costs through rework and waste, while output that meets expectations tends to build repeat sales and reputation.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A chain of consequences runs from product quality through customer retention to revenue and profit: output that keeps meeting expectations tends to hold repeat sales and word-of-mouth, which supports revenue, though profit still depends on the cost of achieving that quality.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: All types of business - manufacturers, retailers and service providers - are affected by quality, because the customer's test of fitness for purpose applies to a welded gate, a bag of maize meal and a bank transaction in the same way.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Quality control is the checking of finished output against a standard, usually at the end of production by appointed inspectors, so that defective units are found before they reach the customer.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business implements quality control by setting a standard for the finished product, inspecting output against that standard at the end of the process, and rejecting, reworking or scrapping units that fail.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Inspecting at the end of the process carries costs: the defect has already absorbed full materials and labour before it is found, and a repaired unit carries extra cost and delay, so late detection tends to cost more than getting the stage right first time.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Quality assurance is the prevention of quality problems across the whole production process, built on the commitment of every worker to quality at every stage, so that errors are stopped before they occur rather than caught at the end.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business implements quality assurance through methods such as quality circles, staff training and quality systems, which aim to build quality into each stage rather than inspect it in at the end.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A quality assurance approach tends to cut waste and rework costs because errors are prevented during production rather than discovered in finished output, though setting it up takes time and training cost.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Quality control checks output at the end of production by appointed inspectors, whereas quality assurance prevents faults across the whole process through every worker's commitment; both aim at the customer receiving output that meets expectations, but they work at different points in the process.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
